title: Championship clubs vote to replace PSR with squad cost ratio financial rules
content:
Championship clubs have voted to introduce a squad-cost ratio (SCR) regime from next season, in a move that brings their approach to financial regulation in line with the Premier League’s.

The new system, which limits clubs to spending a maximum of 85 per cent of their revenues on their first-team squads, will replace the profitability and sustainability rules (PSR) that have been in place since 2017.

With a two-thirds majority needed to make the change, there had been some doubt that enough clubs were in favour of swapping SCR for PSR. In fact, when the matter was put to an indicative vote last month, only 15 clubs were in favour, with six against and three abstentions. But Friday’s vote was decisive, with 20 clubs in favour and only four opposed.

Under the new regime, squad costs are defined as all wages for first-team players and coaching staff, plus amortised transfer costs and agents fees.

There is also one key difference between the Championship’s version of SCR and the Premier League’s, as Championship club owners will be allowed to top up their revenues with cash injections of up to £33million over a three-year period, but no more than £15million in a single season.

“The new framework allows for real-time monitoring during the season, rather than reviewing ‘after the event’, with the aim of giving clubs greater clarity and (the EFL’s) Club Financial Reporting Unit earlier visibility over clubs’ financial positions,” an EFL statement explained.

“The changes are intended to create a simpler and more responsive system of cost control within the Championship.”

The PSR regime was based on limiting the amount of money each club could lose over a rolling three-season period. Clubs were able to exclude costs related to community work, infrastructure improvements, the women’s team and youth development, but were not allowed to lose more than £39m over three years once those deductions had been made.

Over the nine years PSR was in operation in the EFL, several clubs were sanctioned for breaching that threshold, with Birmingham City, Derby County, Leicester City, Reading and Sheffield Wednesday all receiving points-deductions.

Despite UEFA using SCR since 2022, support for the approach has not been unanimous in either the Premier League or the Championship. When the top flight voted on it in November, only 14 of the 20 clubs backed it.

Those opposed to SCR believe it favours clubs with the largest revenues, as opposed to ones that try to run themselves sustainably.

Another concern with the EFL has been the potential widening of the financial gap between the Championship and League One, where clubs have voted to tighten their existing version of SCR, which is called the Salary Cost Management Protocol (SCMP).

For the last few seasons, League One clubs have been allowed to spend up to 60 per cent of their turnover on player wages but that will be reduced to 50 per cent next season, with “manager costs” also now included in the SCMP equation.

As now, clubs relegated to League One will be given more flexibility while they reduce their wage bills, but their limit has also been reduced, coming down from 75 per cent of turnover to 65 per cent.

In a further change designed to reverse the division’s recent spike in losses, League One clubs also voted to treat equity injections on the same 50 per cent basis, meaning that any owner who puts £1million into their club next season, will only be allowed to spend £500,000 of it on wages.

This greatly simplifies what was a complicated “staggered” approach to cash injections, which allowed 100 per cent of the first £500,000 to be included as revenue, with 75 per cent of the next £250,000 permitted and 60 per cent of the rest allowed. This move is intended to encourage spending on other areas, such as the stadium, training ground or youth development.

League Two clubs, however, rejected a proposal to mirror League One’s approach to equity injections, which means the “staggered” method will continue to apply.
